title: The Ocean's Floating Lid
question: How does a layer of frozen seawater shape the climate of the whole planet?
hook: Ice covering about 12% of the world's oceans helps decide how warm the entire Earth gets.
idea: Sea ice cools the planet by reflecting sunlight and insulating the ocean, and it shifts with wind, currents and the seasons.

beats.prompt: You freeze a jar of salty seawater, pop out the block and drop it into the sea. What happens?

choices.label: It sinks, because salt makes it heavy
choices.feedback: Salt and brine are trapped inside, but frozen water is still less dense than liquid water overall.

choices.label: It hangs halfway down, neither rising nor sinking
choices.feedback: Ice is less dense than the water around it, so it rises until it floats.

beats.explain: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so sea ice floats on the ocean surface just as freshwater ice does.

beats.prompt: Put these stages of sea ice in order, from just frozen to oldest
beats.explain: Scientists sort sea ice by its development stage: new ice, then nilas, young ice, first-year ice and finally old ice.

beats.prompt: Sort each description into the kind of sea ice it fits
items: Held in place by grounded icebergs
Free to move with currents and winds
Spread across very wide offshore areas
beats.explain: Fast ice is attached to the shore, shoals or grounded icebergs; drift ice lies further offshore, moves freely and is made of floes.

beats.prompt: Match each floe name to its size across
beats.explain: Floes, the separate pieces of drift ice, get named by width, from small at 20 m up to giant beyond 10 km.
